claims.claim: Isaac (60) and Rebekah, after barrenness and prayer, have twin sons; the twins struggle in the womb; Rebekah inquires of the LORD and receives the oracle "the elder shall serve the younger" (Gen 25:19–26, 23). Esau is born red and hairy; Jacob follows grasping his heel.
*bĕkōrâ* (H1062) = "right of first-born" (BDB); occurrences Gen 25:31–34, 27:36, 43:33; Deut 21:17; 1 Chr 5:1–2.
claims.evidence: BDB, *bĕkōrâ* (BibleHub BDB section, read 2026-11-17). BDB also lists "Gen 23:34" — an apparent misprint for 25:34; not cited.

claims.claim: In the narrative the birthright is the double share and the headship of the family (Skinner, citing Deut 21:17), transferable by legal fiction (1 Chr 5:1–2); the idea of a spiritual privilege, and the Heb 12:16 reading, are foreign to the ancient legends.
Esau sells his birthright for bread and lentil pottage, confirmed by oath; the narrator's verdict is "thus Esau despised his birthright" (Gen 25:29–34).

The saga asks how the firstborn right passed from Esau to Jacob and answers: bought for a trifle. Esau's "let me swallow some of the red" is drastic humour; he probably does not know they are lentils. The Edom gloss (25:30b) is likely a gloss.
*bĕrākâ* (H1293) = "blessing" (BDB): of a parent (Gen 27:12, 41); "the blessing of Abraham" (*birkat ʾAbraham*, Gen 28:4); also "a gift, present" (Gen 33:11).
Isaac's blessing (27:27–29) is partly natural, partly political, concerned with the future greatness of Israel; "peoples... nations" = the neighbours subdued by David (2 Sam 8).

A spoken paternal blessing, once given, could not be withdrawn: it was not subjective affection but a right entrusted by grace to paternal authority, guided by a higher authority (K&D); Isaac confirms "yea, he shall be blessed" (27:33; cf. Heb 12:17).

Esau's blessing (27:39–40) is "a modified curse" (K&D); *min* in 27:39 is privative ("away from the fat places") against partitive in 27:28; "break his yoke" (27:40b) may be a later addition reflecting Edom's emancipation (2 Kgs 8:20–22 or 16:6).
claims.evidence: K&D Gen 27 (privative *min*); Skinner pp. 368–375 (double entendre misled the LXX; 27:40b as later addition). The *min* reading is contested.

claims.claim: Paul (Rom 9:10–13) reads the prenatal choice of Jacob over Esau as grace before birth or works; Augustine (XVI.35) records the near-unanimous patristic reading (elder people = Jews serving younger = Christians) while noting the Idumaean fulfilment.
claims.evidence: Augustine, *City of God* XVI.35 (read in full); Rom 9:10–13 (KJV).

claims.claim: The name Jacob (*Yaʿkub-ilu*) is attested in a Hammurabi-age Babylonian contract tablet and in Thothmes III's list (No. 102), also in Ramses II/III lists.
*ʿāqab* (H6117) = "follow at the heel; figuratively assail insidiously, circumvent, overreach" (denominative from *ʿāqēb*); Gen 27:36 "he hath overreached me now twice"; Hos 12:4; Jer 9:3.

Gen 27 is NOT an "oral will" with legal force, and no Nuzi text supports arbitrary determination of the birthright. HSS 5 48 is bedside witness evidence to identify the eldest son, not an appointment of chief heir; AASOR 16 56 concerns a father's oral statement about his youngest son's marriage; HSS 9 34 concerns tenancy and land. None of the three has anything to do with paternal blessings, the real subject of Gen 27.
claims.evidence: Selman (1976) 128–132 (read in full); cf. Speiser, JBL 74 (1955) 252–256 (cited via Selman, not read directly).

claims.claim: Jacob flees Beersheba for Haran, sleeps at "the place", dreams of a *sullam* with angels ascending and descending, hears the promise (land, seed, presence, return), awakes, anoints the stone, names the place Bethel ("House of God"), and vows a tithe (Gen 28:10–22).
*sullām* (H5551) = "ladder" (BDB); sole OT occurrence, Gen 28:12; from the root *s-l-l* ("to heap up, cast up, pave").
claims.evidence: BDB, *sullām* (BibleHub BDB section, read 2026-11-17). **Correction:** H5556 is *salʿam*, "bald locust" (Lev 11:22) — not *sullām*.

claims.claim: Houtman's thesis: the *sullam* is probably the ascent/slope of the mountain of Bethel, the later high place — the "way" giving entry to the sanctuary; "Jacob was sleeping on the *sullam*"; the rocks around Jacob are not transformed into a staircase in his dream.
claims.evidence: Houtman (1977) 337–351 (read in full). Minority thesis; see debated-questions register Q1.

claims.claim: The ladder/stairway reading: LXX *klimax* and Vulgate *scala* can each mean ladder or staircase; the translators probably thought of a ladder, inaugurating a long tradition. Ziggurat readings (Henderson, Bohl, Jeremias, von Rad) relate the *sullam* to Mesopotamian temple-towers; Houtman finds no reason to relate it to the ziggurat. The Akkadian *simmiltu* ("staircase") is used for communication between heaven and the netherworld.
claims.evidence: Houtman (1977) 337–351 (read in full; Henderson, Bohl, Jeremias, Keller, van Selms, von Rad cited via Houtman).

claims.claim: "Gate of heaven" (28:17): Houtman — Jacob was sleeping IN the gate, at the domicile of Yahweh; heaven and earth melt into one at the holy place; "house of God" means the real presence of God on earth.

*maṣṣēbâ* (H4676) = "pillar"; a stone set up and anointed as memorial of divine appearance (Gen 28:18, 22; 31:13; 35:14); set up in token of agreement (Gen 31:45, 51–52); set up over a grave (Gen 35:20). Canaanite pillars are later condemned (Deut 16:22).

The stone at Bethel: Skinner — the stone was the abode of a deity; the *maṣṣēbâ* was originally a fetish, later a symbol or memorial; anointing stones is widely attested (Pausanias x.24.6, Delphi; *baetyl*/*betyl*; the Canaanite deity Bethel attested Assyriologically). Luz is distinct from Bethel (Josh 16:2; 18:13). Bethel = modern Beitin, ~10 miles north of Jerusalem.

Bethel = Beitin (5 km NE of Ramallah): identified by Robinson (1838–52), reaffirmed by Tristram; the minority al-Bireh proposal is rejected by excavation workers. MB II (c. 1750 BCE) fortified Canaanite town believed to be biblical Luz; LB city destroyed late 13th/early 12th century BCE; excavations Albright 1927, Albright & Kelso 1934–60. No excavated feature can be tied to the Jacob narratives.
claims.evidence: Wikipedia "Bethel" (accessed 2026-11-17; article crawled 2026-10-02). Secondary summary of excavation reports not read directly — hence Probable, not Established.

claims.claim: Rashi (28:12): the angels ascending first were those who accompanied Jacob in the Land and could not leave it; they ascended, and angels for outside the Land descended (Gen. Rabbah 68:12).
claims.evidence: Rashi on Gen 28:12 (Sefaria, read 2026-11-17); Gen. Rabbah cited via Rashi.

claims.claim: Philo (*De Somniis* I.133–163) gives four readings of the ladder: (1) the air, abode of incorporeal souls/angels; (2) the soul in man; (3) the practiser of virtue's life; (4) the affairs of mankind. God stands above as charioteer/pilot; God is "God and Lord of Abraham, but only God of Isaac" — Abraham symbolises knowledge from teaching, Isaac knowledge by nature.
claims.evidence: Philo, *De Somniis* I (Yonge trans., read in full §§133–163).

claims.claim: Augustine (XVI.38): Jacob did not anoint the stone idolatrously; since Christ's name comes from *chrism*/anointing, "something pertaining to the great mystery was certainly represented in this". John 1:47, 51: Nathanael "an Israelite indeed, in whom is no guile"; angels ascending and descending on the Son of Man.
claims.evidence: Augustine, *City of God* XVI.38 (read in full); John 1:47, 51 (KJV).

claims.claim: Houtman: Gen 28:12 is a "Kontrastparallele" of Gen 11:4 (Babel): man builds a citadel "into the heaven" from earth; at Bethel the ascent is set towards the earth — communication established by initiative from on high, by grace. The emphasis of the narration is vv. 13–15, especially v. 15: God renews the promise and assures nearness even outside Canaan.

Seven years' service for Rachel instead of *mōhar* (bride-price) was recognised by ancient Arabs; the first cousin's prior right obtained among Bedouin and Egyptians; Laban substitutes Leah, and Jacob serves seven more years (Gen 29:15–30).
"Hated" (29:31) is a technical term for the less-favoured wife (Deut 21:15), not emotional hatred.

"Bear upon my knees" (30:3) is NOT adoption but birth, naming, and welcome by the family: the phrase occurs in two Hurrian tales (Ullikummi myth; Appu myth — "The nurse lifted up the boy and set him on Appu's knees") and in a Neo-Assyrian blessing ("May the king, my lord, lift his grandsons upon his knees", cf. Gen 48:12; 50:23). Skinner's reading (primitive adoption ceremony, cf. Job 3:12; Iliad ix.455f; Odyssey xix.901ff.) is the older view.
claims.evidence: Selman (1976) 124–125 (read in full) vs Skinner pp. 386–389. Preserve both.

claims.claim: The barren wife's slavegirl (Gen 16; 30:1–13) matches HSS 5 67 (Nuzi adoption contract) in three elements — barrenness as cause, the wife's initiative, the wife's authority — BUT the same practice appears in Hammurabi §§144 and 163 and in an Old Babylonian contract (Schorr No. 77); HSS 5 67 is the sole Nuzi example; and ND 2307 (Nimrud, late 7th century) shows the same basic custom in the first millennium. The custom cannot fix a date.
claims.evidence: Selman (1976) 122–124 (read in full). Hammurabi §§144, 163 and ND 2307 cited via Selman (not read directly this session); the registry entry for the Hammurabi Code is verified from earlier work.

claims.claim: The tribal etymologies in Gen 29:31–30:24 are "extremely forced" (Skinner); Dan's etymology (*dîn*, "judge") is very probably correct; Gad is the Aramaean/Phoenician god of Luck (Isa 65:11); Asher is possibly related to Asherah.
Mandrakes (*dûdāʾîm*) = *Mandragora vernalis* fruit, ripening in May, sought to promote conception; the story is curtailed (Wellhausen).

The flocks (30:25–43): two conceptions of reward are fused (J vs E); parti-coloured animals are a very small proportion (Syrian sheep nearly all white, goats black or brown); the rods are poplar (*libneh*, *Styrax officinalis*), almond (*lûz*), and plane tree; stronger sheep conceived in summer and yeaned in winter (Pliny, *NH* viii.187).

Rachel did NOT steal the teraphim to secure Jacob's inheritance (Selman, following Greenberg, JBL 81 (1962) 239–248): of 11 Nuzi references to household gods, in 9 the gods are part of an inheritance — but in each case other heirs who did NOT receive the gods also shared; possession did not equal an automatic claim; a just claim depended on proper bequeathal. Jacob wanted distance from Laban, not his property; his wealth came from wages (Gen 31:1–9).
claims.evidence: Selman (1976) 118–121 (read in full). Greenberg cited via Selman (not read directly).

claims.claim: The *errebu*-marriage does not exist: the only occurrences are the verb *erebu* ("to enter") in the Assyrian laws and an emended *ana ittisu*; the abstract *errebutu* occurs on no tablet. There is no evidence Jacob only visited his wives in Laban's house or that Laban adopted him to marry Leah and Rachel.

"To eat money" (Gen 31:15) = Nuzi *kaspa akalu* (dowry kept in trust by the bride's father, enjoying its income); in Nuzi the phrase occurs five times, mainly in adoption contracts, where the guardian keeps the whole sum — consistent in both.

The second-wife restriction (Gen 31:50) has a genuine parallel, but it is not confined to Nuzi: it is found in marriage contracts across the ancient Near East from the Old Assyrian period onward. In Genesis it is not in a marriage contract at all — Jacob had married Leah thirteen years and Rachel six years earlier.

*tĕrāphîm* (H8655): "a kind of idol, object of reverence, and means of divination" (BDB); portable and sometimes small (Gen 31:19, 34–35 — called *ʾĕlōhîm*, "gods", 31:30), but man-sized in 1 Sam 19:13, 16; household shrine (Judg 17:5; 18:14–20; Hos 3:4); condemned (1 Sam 15:23; 2 Kgs 23:24); used in divining (Ezek 21:21).
claims.evidence: BDB, *tĕrāphîm* (BibleHub BDB section, read 2026-11-17); Skinner pp. 396–399 on the teraphim as a god used in divination and an emblem of ancestor-worship.

claims.claim: The treaty of Gilead (31:43–55) is a double recension: Gilead/Mizpah, cairn/monolith, family compact (E) vs frontier treaty (J). Gilead = Jebel ʿAjlūn and el-Belka; the name Jebel Jilʿād survives (Jebel Oshaʿ north of es-Salt). Mizpah is east of Jordan, possibly Ramoth-gilead — "precarious". The Syrian-wars background theory (Wellhausen, c. 860–770 BCE) is met by Gunkel's objection (it reads like a loose understanding between friendly tribes).
"The Fear of Isaac" = the deity feared by Isaac; Meyer's speculation that it is a Beersheba local deity is "hazardous".

Joseph is born to Rachel (30:22–24), closing the Laban cycle; Gen 30:25 follows immediately with Jacob's request to leave. Joseph's birth is the bridge to the next category (Joseph and Israel in Egypt, Gen 37–50), not duplicated there.

Mahanaim = "double camp/host"; the host of God joined Jacob's host as safeguard. Its site is placed at Mahne on Wadi el-Himar, ~14 miles north of the Jabbok; the Jabbok is the Nahr ez-Zerka; the ford itself is unidentified (Mukhaḍat en-Nuṣrānīyeh suggested). Mahanaim later became Ish-bosheth's capital, David's headquarters in Absalom's revolt, and a fiscal district under Solomon.
claims.evidence: Skinner pp. 408–411 (read in full); Ryle on Gen 32 (read in full).

claims.claim: Esau comes with 400 men (32:7); his purpose — hostile or friendly — is unresolved: "truth between extremes" (Skinner). Josephus says Esau was "very glad" and met his brother with 400 men; Jacob divided his company and sent presents at intervals so they would appear more numerous.

Jacob's prayer (32:9–12) has four parts: (1) invocation; (2) reminder of the promise; (3) humble acknowledgment of mercies; (4) entreaty for protection and fulfilment of the covenant promise. "I am not worthy" = Hebrew "I am less than all" — too small and insignificant to deserve. Prayer plus wrestling mark a character made ready through discipline for faith and submission.
claims.evidence: Ryle on Gen 32 (read in full); KJV Gen 32:9–12.

claims.claim: The wrestling (32:24–32): *ʾāḇaq* is chosen for assonance with *Yaʿăqōb*; the dislocation is twice recorded (two sources); "let me go, for the dawn is breaking" preserves the belief in night-spirits vanishing at dawn (Plautus, *Amphitruo* 532f; *Hamlet* I.i).

Rashi (32:25): Jacob had returned for forgotten small jars (Chullin 91a); *wayyēʾāḇēq* — Menachem ben Saruk explains "a man covered himself with dust" (from *ʾāḇāq*, dust); Rashi reads "he fastened himself on" (Aramaic, "intertwining"). The Rabbis explained the wrestler was Esau's guardian angel (Gen. Rabbah 77:3).
claims.evidence: Rashi on Gen 32:25 (Sefaria, read 2026-11-17); Gen. Rabbah and Chullin cited via Rashi.

claims.claim: Onkelos (Gen 32) renders *wayyēʾāḇēq* as *ishtadel* ("strove, wrestled"); 32:29 softens "with God" to "are great before God"; 32:31 renders *Elohim* as "Angels of God"; 32:26 "he struck the socket [girth] of his hip". Onkelos does NOT use a *k-m-n* form at 32:25 — Rashi's Targum citation of *wḥkmny* belongs to 27:36, not 32:25.
claims.evidence: Targum Onkelos Gen 32 (Sefaria, read in full 2026-11-17).

claims.claim: *yiśrāʾēl* (H3478): "El persisteth, persevereth (or jussive Let El persist); usually contendeth or Let El contend" (BDB); Egyptian *Y-si-r-'l* (Steindorff, ZAW 1896). Skinner: probably "God strives", interpreted "Striver with God"; cf. Yerubbaʿal (Judg 6:32); Driver: Arabic *sariya*, "persist, persevere"; Merneptah inscription *Ysiraʾr*.

Gunkel: the wrestler is a hostile being lurking "like a panther by the way" at the ford, perhaps the numen of the river, angry because Jacob crosses his ford; "This god is certainly not Yahweh — Yahweh is the god who loves and helps Jacob". Parallels: Menelaus holding Proteus (Od. IV.384ff.); Midas capturing Silenus; Numa capturing Faunus and Picus.

Keil & Delitzsch: the wrestler is God in the Angel of Jehovah (Hos 12:4–5) — not a created angel but the visible manifestation of the invisible God; not a dream or internal vision but within the sphere of sensuous perception; a "real conflict of both mind and body". Jacob overcame God not with the power of the flesh but by faith and prayer, holding fast till blessed.

Augustine (XVI.39): the angel was "most evidently a type of Christ"; Jacob overcame him "doubtless with his own consent, that the mystery might be represented, it signified Christ's passion, in which the Jews are seen overcoming Him". "Israel means seeing God, which will at last be the reward of all the saints." The thigh-touch made Jacob lame — blessed in believers, lame in unbelievers; "the breadth of the thigh is the multitude of the family".
claims.evidence: Augustine, *City of God* XVI.39 (read in full).

claims.claim: *pĕnîʾēl / pĕnûʾēl* (H6439) = "face of God"; location east of Jordan near the Jabbok (Gen 32:31–32; Judg 8:8, 9, 17; 1 Kgs 12:25); site unknown.

The meeting (Gen 33): the sevenfold prostration is the Amarna formula ("At the feet of my Lord, my Sun, I fall down seven and seven times") but does not imply vassalage; "seen thy face, as though I had seen the face of God" is a flattering comparison (1 Sam 29:9; 2 Sam 14:17, 19:27), possibly a reminiscence of Peniel; the change of tone — Esau now noble and princely, Jacob shrewd but not knavish — may come from sanctuaries frequented by Israelites and Edomites in common (Holzinger).
*bĕrākâ* as "gift, present": Jacob's present to Esau is called "my blessing" (Gen 33:11).
"Wrought folly in Israel" (*nebalâ*, 34:7) is a standing phrase for sexual crimes (Deut 22:21; Judg 20:6, 10; 2 Sam 13:12); "in Israel" is an anachronism.
claims.evidence: Skinner pp. 418–433 (read in full); K&D Gen 34 (standing phrase for crimes against the honour and calling of Israel, esp. shameful sins of the flesh).

claims.claim: Gen 34 is two recensions (J* and E*) plus Priestly redaction; circumcision is a pretext (E*) vs a good-faith compact violated by Simeon and Levi alone (J*). Material difficulties: the children are grown up; Jacob is not "Israel" in J after 32:28; Jacob is not west of Jordan in J; the sons feed flocks at Shechem (37:12).

Simeon and Levi are called "brothers of Dinah" — yet Leah had four other equally full brothers: another tradition may have had Simeon and Levi as the only sons of Leah (Meyer). Jacob rebukes their recklessness, not their treachery or cruelty.

Gunkel's tribal-historical reading: the persons are brother-tribes; Shechem is the eponym of a Canaanite city; Hamor is the name of a Canaanite (Hivite, v. 2) clan dwelling at Shechem (cf. Judg 9:28). The sons live as nomads (vv. 5, 7, 10, 21) while Shechem and Hamor live in houses and in a city. Probably an event of Israelite prehistory echoes: brother-tribes surprised Shechem, the city stayed Canaanite, the other tribes remained neutral. Gen 49:5–7 preserves a third variant (cunning attack, curse, scattering).

Dinah appears only three times in the Hebrew Bible (Gen 34; 30:21; 46:15); she is the subject of an action only once; she never speaks; she never appears again. *Wayeʿanneha* (34:2) is more precisely "debased" — a downward social movement (cf. Gen 16:6) — not necessarily forced sex; seduction is the alternative reading. The narrative reserves judgment; there is no indication the characters are concerned with Dinah's well-being — the shame is to the family, not (explicitly) to her.

Deut 22:28–29 and Exod 22:15 require marriage after such an act (for the woman's and family's benefit); the Bible never depicts these laws as carried out. Middle Assyrian Laws 55–56 (11th century BCE) are a parallel. The story shows strong opposition to exogamy, common in postexilic literature (Ezra–Nehemiah; cf. Deut 7; Josh 23:12; Ezra 9:14); Ruth takes the opposite view.

Jubilees 30: Dinah is "a little girl, a child of twelve years"; Simeon and Levi slew all the men "in torments because they had dishonoured their sister"; laws against intermarriage follow; "Levi [was] chosen for the priesthood on account of his slaughter of the Shechemites" (vv. 18–23). Jubilees omits the circumcision of the Shechemites, as does Josephus. In the two centuries before the Christian era the act was highly extolled (Test. Levi 5–7; Judith 9:2; Philo, *De Migr.* 39); late rabbinic tradition judges them more harshly, per Gen 49 (Gen. Rabbah 80; Sifre Deut 33:8).
claims.evidence: Jubilees 30 (Charles trans., read in full 2026-11-17). Test. Levi, Judith, Philo *De Migr.*, Gen. Rabbah, Sifre — **second-hand** via Charles's note (not read directly).

claims.claim: Shechem = Tell Balata (valley between Mount Ebal and Mount Gerizim): MB II fortified Canaanite town (first substantial building c. 1900 BC; MB IIB temples, Wall D; MB IIC Fortress Temple, walls ~5 m thick). Attested in Egyptian sources (Sebek-khu stele, Senusret III; Amarna EA 289; Papyrus Anastasi I). Break in occupation c. 1150–975 BC. Archaeology neither confirms nor refutes Gen 34.
claims.evidence: Wikipedia "Shechem" (accessed 2026-11-17; article crawled 2026-11-15). Secondary summary — hence Probable.

claims.claim: Deborah's death (35:8) is perplexing: the nurse is nameless in 24:59, and how she came into Jacob's family is inexplicable. The sacred tree is probably identical with the palm of Deborah (Judg 4:5) — a confusion between prophetess and nurse; Cheyne: "oak of weeping" is perhaps "Tree of Rebekah".

Rachel dies (35:16–20): Ephrath is an unknown locality in later Benjamin territory; "that is Bethlehem" is a gloss (Stade). Rachel's grave is determined by 1 Sam 10:2 (border of Benjamin, between Ramah and Gibeah) and Jer 31:15 — the Christian tradition ~1 mile north of Bethlehem rests on a confusion of Ephrath with the clan-name Ephrathah. *Ben-oni* = "son of my sorrow"; Benjamin is probably "son of the south".

Reuben and Bilhah (35:22a): the story went on to a curse explaining the loss of the birthright (Gunkel; cf. 49:4); parallel Iliad ix.449ff (Phoenix). Ethnographic reading: the humiliation of the Bilhah-tribe (Dan or Naphtali).

Gen 36 (seven/eight sections) embodies authentic information about the history and ethnology of Edom; Meyer's hypothesis of a native Edomite literature behind it is credible. The wives' name differences (36:2–3 vs 26:34; 28:9) are the result of a redactional process / divergence within the Priestly school.

The kings list (36:31–39), "before there reigned any king over the children of Israel", has as its terminus the overthrow of Edomite independence by David; it "bears every mark of authenticity" and is presumed complete; with an average reign of 20 years (Meyer) the monarchy runs ~150–200 years before David; it is not hereditary — the kings reign in different cities, analogous to the Hebrew Judges as local chiefs (Winckler, Cheyne).

Bela son of Beor resembles Balaam son of Beor (Num 22–24; Num 31:8) — their identity is recognised by Knobel-Dillmann, Nöldeke, Hommel, Sayce, and Cheyne; Pethor on the Euphrates is inconsistent with the identification.
Jobab of Bozrah: the LXX identifies him with the patriarch Job (Job 42:17 LXX); Bozrah is now el-Buseireh, 20 miles SE of the Dead Sea.
claims.evidence: Skinner pp. 434–439 (read in full). The LXX identification is tradition, not evidence; the site identification is probable.

claims.claim: Hadad son of Bedad, "who smote Midian in the field of Moab" (36:35), is a solitary historical notice; Ewald reads it as an incident of a great Midianite raid, contemporary with Gideon. No independent corroboration exists.
claims.evidence: Skinner pp. 434–439 (read in full). Single notice only.

claims.claim: Amalek: son of Timna, concubine of Eliphaz; ancestor of the Amalekites who attacked at Rephidim (Ex 17:8); NOT an aboriginal nation (the Arabic legend of Amlik is too recent, confused, and contradictory); "first of the nations" (Num 24:20) = the first heathen tribe by which Israel was attacked; Gen 14:7 "field of the Amalekites" does not imply the tribe existed in Abraham's time.

The Edomite kingdom flourished 13th–8th centuries BC; capital Bozrah; attested in Egyptian sources (Seti I list c. 1215 BC; Ramesses III campaign; Papyrus Anastasi VI — "shasu-tribes of Edom" admitted to Wadi Tumilat under Merneptah); Assyrian kings Kaus-malaka (Tiglath-pileser III, c. 745 BC), Aya-ramu (Sennacherib, c. 705 BC), Kaus-gabri (Esarhaddon, c. 680 BC); conquered by Nabonidus c. 553 BC.
claims.evidence: Wikipedia "Edom" (accessed 2026-11-17; article crawled 2026-11-05). Secondary summary — hence Probable.

claims.claim: Khirbat en-Nahas (Wadi Faynan) is one of the largest ancient copper mining/smelting sites, built ~3,000 years ago; Levy argues its scale could have been organised only by "an ancient state or kingdom"; Ben-Yosef & Levy 2019 (copper samples from Timna and Faynan dated 1300–800 BC) argue for a centralised 10th-century BC Edomite kingdom. The political interpretation is contested.
claims.evidence: Wikipedia "Khirbat en-Nahas" (accessed 2026-11-17; article crawled 2026-06-30) and Wikipedia "Edom". Secondary summaries — hence Debated.

claims.claim: *ʾĕdôm* (H123): (1) "name of a condiment", Gen 25:30 (twice); (2) proper name Edom = Esau, Gen 25:30 (etymology = red, cf. 25:25), 36:1, 8, 19; collective Edomites, Gen 36:9, 43; land of Edom, Gen 36:32, 43; "field of Edom" (*śĕdēh ʾĕdôm*), Gen 32:4.

The Horites were previously an independent people (Gen 14:6), partly exterminated and partly subjugated by Esau's descendants (Deut 2:12, 22); Timna is probably the same as the concubine of Eliphaz (36:12); Aholibamah (36:25) is not Esau's wife.

connections.note: The Abrahamic promise (land, seed, blessing to all families) that is renewed to Isaac (26:2–5, 24) and to Jacob (28:13–15; 35:9–13). Gen 12 has 20 verses.
"In Isaac shall thy seed be called" — the narrowing of the line through Isaac, cited by Augustine (XVI.38) for the separation of Jacob's seed from Esau's. Gen 21 has 34 verses.
Rebekah's journey and marriage to Isaac — the preceding category's close; the entry point to Isaac's *toledoth* (25:19). Gen 24 has 67 verses.
Joseph sold by his brothers — the bridge to the next category (Joseph and Israel in Egypt); Joseph's birth (30:22–24) is in this category, his sale in the next. Gen 37 has 36 verses.
Jacob goes down to Egypt with his household; Augustine (XVI.40) notes the 75 souls count the whole period Joseph lived, not one day. Gen 46 has 34 verses.
Jacob crosses his hands, blessing Ephraim above Manasseh — Philo (Leg. All. III.26–27) pairs this with the Jacob/Esau reversal: the younger preferred by design. Gen 48 has 22 verses.
Jacob's words over Reuben (49:3–4, cf. 35:22a) and over Simeon and Levi (49:5–7, the Shechem judgment) — the retrospective verdict on Gen 34 and Gen 35:22. Gen 49 has 33 verses.
Judah's blessing, expounded by Augustine (XVI.41) against Faustus: the lion, the robe washed in wine. Gen 49 has 33 verses.
The firstborn's double portion, which cannot be transferred by paternal favouritism — the legal background to the birthright (Skinner on 29:31; BDB on *bĕkōrâ*). Deut 21 has 23 verses.
The law requiring marriage after the seizure of an unbetrothed virgin — the legal context for the Dinah episode discussed by Bible Odyssey ("Dinah"). Deut 22 has 30 verses (verified live 2026-11-17).
"Thou shalt not abhor an Edomite; for he is thy brother" — the later legal memory of the Jacob/Esau brotherhood. Deut 23 has 25 verses.
Penuel's tower thrown down by Gideon — the later history of the place Jacob named Peniel (32:31). Judg 8 has 35 verses.
David subdues Edom — the fulfilment of the blessing's dominion (27:29) and the oracle's "elder shall serve younger" (Bible Odyssey "Jacob"). 2 Sam 8 has 18 verses.
Amnon and Tamar — the closest biblical parallel to Dinah: the same word *nebalâ*, a brother's vengeance, a father's inaction (Bible Odyssey "Dinah"). 2 Sam 13 has 39 verses.
Edom revolts under Jehoram and breaks the yoke — the fulfilment of 27:40b ("thou shalt break his yoke from off thy neck"). 2 Kgs 8 has 29 verses.
The birthright given to Joseph after Reuben defiled his father's bed (cf. 35:22a; 49:4) — the transfer of the birthright by legal fiction. 1 Chr 5 has 26 verses.
"He took his brother by the heel in the womb, and by his strength he had power with God" — the prophet's summary of Gen 25:26 and Gen 32. Hos 12 has 14 verses.
The oracle against Edom — the whole book is the prophetic sequel to the Jacob/Esau rivalry. Obadiah has 21 verses.
"Jacob have I loved, but Esau have I hated" — the prophetic echo of the election in Gen 25:23. Mal 1 has 14 verses.
Nathanael, "an Israelite indeed, in whom is no guile"; the angels ascending and descending on the Son of Man — Augustine's (XVI.38) reading of the Bethel ladder. John 1 has 51 verses.
The election of Jacob over Esau before birth or works — Paul's reading of Gen 25:23, the centre of Augustine XVI.35. Rom 9 has 33 verses.
"By faith Isaac blessed Jacob and Esau concerning things to come" — the NT's verdict on the blessing. Heb 11 has 40 verses.
Esau the "profane person" who sold his birthright for one morsel of meat and found no place of repentance — the NT's verdict on Gen 25:29–34 and 27:34. Heb 12 has 29 verses.

Rabbah 80:1, recorded only to be recognised, never repeated as fact) — FLAGGED for Yonatan: whether to name the sexual-violence question at all on a public page, and how much prominence the ‘debased’ vs ‘rape’ wording receives; D2 Simeon/Levi presented in the text's own order (narrative silence, then Jubilees 30 extolling, then Gen 49:5–7 cursing; Jacob's rebuke in 34:30 concerns danger, not morality), no reading foregrounded; D3 Jacob's character framed by the narrative arc first (deceiver, victim of deception, shrewd negotiator, fearful fugitive, reconciled brother), then Gunkel/Skinner, Augustine (XVI.37), and K&D side by side, none leading as ‘the’ interpretation; D4 Houtman's mountain-slope thesis (EM-decided 2026-11-17): ladder as the traditional reading, Houtman in one brief sentence as a debated minority alternative; D5 Reuben/Bilhah in one sentence, not foregrounded (35:22a; Gen 49:4; the Bilhah-tribe ethnographic reading as Debated); D6 no override needed (resolved).
